name: Hippocrates Diet

card.summary: A raw, plant-based 'living foods' regimen built around wheatgrass and sprouts, taught by the Hippocrates Health Institute and followed by people who want clearer skin, leanness and general vitality.
card.aka: Living foods diet, Hippocrates Health Program
card.note: Its founders and institute have been the subject of regulatory action and criticism over treatment claims; a strict raw vegan diet can be low in some nutrients.

quick.overview:
The Hippocrates Diet is the raw vegan 'living foods' approach associated with Ann Wigmore and the Hippocrates Health Institute, which she co-founded with Viktoras Kulvinskas in 1956 [1][2]. It centers on uncooked plant foods, sprouts and wheatgrass juice.

People who follow it describe wanting a lean body and clear, healthy-looking skin from a diet high in fresh vegetables and low in processed food. Research on the diet itself is thin, and its institutional history includes legal disputes over medical claims [1][2].
quick.how: Followers eat uncooked plant foods, often including sprouted seeds and grains and juiced wheatgrass, and avoid animal products and processed items. Wigmore's books, including The Wheatgrass Book (1985), spread the practice [2].
quick.risks: Critics describe Wigmore's detoxification claims for wheatgrass and chlorophyll as erroneous, and the institute has been criticized for promoting unproven natural treatments for serious illness [1][2]. In 2015 Florida regulators issued, then withdrew, cease-and-desist orders against its co-directors [1]. Strict raw vegan eating can leave gaps in some nutrients, which is a general nutrition concern rather than a finding specific to this program.

lead: The Hippocrates Diet is a raw, vegan 'living foods' regimen promoted by the Hippocrates Health Institute, a nonprofit now in West Palm Beach, Florida, co-founded in 1956 in Stoneham, Massachusetts, by Viktoras Kulvinskas and Ann Wigmore [1]. Wigmore (1909 to 1994) popularized wheatgrass and other raw foods from the 1940s as a way to detoxify the body [2].

She believed plants held more solar 'Vital Force' than animal foods and that uncooked food eaten soon after harvest kept more of its energy [2]. The approach is the origin of the wheatgrass shot and sprout culture seen in juice bars today.

People interested in appearance follow raw, plant-heavy eating hoping for a lean physique and glowing skin from a diet rich in fresh produce and free of processed foods. Within lifting communities the name mostly appears in passing as a quotation: the line 'let food be thy medicine' is attributed to the ancient physician Hippocrates and quoted in nutrition threads [3][4]. The modern institute and diet are separate from that quotation.

chain: Replace processed food with raw plants and wheatgrass
Lower calorie density and higher produce intake
Leaner body and healthier-looking skin, as followers describe it
angle.text: Followers adopt the diet for a clean, plant-based eating pattern they expect to show in skin clarity and a lean body. These benefits are what proponents describe; they have not been tested in published trials of the program.

paras: Ann Wigmore, a Lithuanian-American naturopath and raw-food advocate, was influenced by Maximilian Bircher-Benner's back-to-nature ideas and promoted wheatgrass and raw foods from the 1940s [2]. The Hippocrates Health Institute grew out of her organization in Boston, and Brian Clement later moved it to West Palm Beach in 1987 [2]. Wigmore wrote around 25 books including The Wheatgrass Book (1985) and died in a house fire in Boston on 16 February 1994 [2].

The institute and Brian Clement have promoted regimens claimed to reverse cancer and multiple sclerosis; critics call those treatments ineffective and possibly dangerous, and note that Clement is not a medical doctor [1]. In February and March 2015 the Florida Department of Health issued cease-and-desist orders to Clement and Anna-Maria Clement for unlicensed practice of medicine, which were later withdrawn and dismissed for lack of sufficient evidence [1].

Wigmore faced legal action too. In 1982 Massachusetts sued over her statements about diabetes and childhood vaccination, which she dropped after losing in court, and in 1988 she was sued over an AIDS claim, with the court barring her from presenting herself as a doctor [2]. Critics describe her wheatgrass detoxification claims as erroneous [2].

In T Nation threads the Hippocratic phrase 'let food be thy medicine' is quoted in discussions of antioxidants and supplements [4], and Hippocrates is cited in debates about diet and health practices [3]. These mentions do not describe the institute's program.

timeline.event: Hippocrates Health Institute co-founded in Stoneham, Massachusetts [1].
Ann Wigmore publishes The Wheatgrass Book [2].
Brian Clement moves the institute to West Palm Beach [2].
Florida issues, then withdraws, cease-and-desist orders against its co-directors [1].

lore.intro: Raw 'living foods' eating is discussed as a detox and vitality regimen; in lifting forums Hippocrates is mostly invoked as a quotation [3][4].

claims.claim: Wheatgrass and raw foods detoxify the body.
claims.believers: Wigmore taught that uncooked plants retain a vital energy and that wheatgrass cleanses the body [2].
claims.experts: Critics describe the chlorophyll detoxification idea as erroneous [2].

claims.claim: The institute's program can reverse serious illness.
claims.believers: The institute and Brian Clement have promoted treatments claimed to reverse cancer and MS [1].
claims.experts: Critics call these treatments ineffective and possibly dangerous; Florida's 2015 orders on unlicensed practice were later withdrawn for insufficient evidence [1].
